title: Dr Reddy's Q1 Profit Drops 69% on Semaglutide Supply Halt, Revlimid Exit
excerpt: The Hyderabad drugmaker booked a Rs 240 crore provision after an API impurity forced it to suspend generic Wegovy production, while the loss of Revlimid revenues and a 35% North America revenue slump compounded the earnings hit.
body:
Dr Reddy's Laboratories reported a 69% decline in consolidated net profit to Rs 443 crore for the first quarter ended June 30, hammered by a double blow: a costly production halt for its generic semaglutide drug and the end of revenues from Lenalidomide, its generic version of Bristol Myers Squibb's blockbuster cancer treatment Revlimid.

The Hyderabad-based company had posted a net profit of Rs 1,418 crore in the year-ago period. Revenue from operations fell 5.6% to Rs 8,070 crore from Rs 8,545 crore, missing the analyst consensus estimate of Rs 8,160 crore. On the NYSE, the company's ADR reported earnings per share of $0.06, missing the $0.09 consensus by $0.03, according to LSEG data.

The Semaglutide Stumble

The quarter's most damaging development was an impurity discovered in Dr Reddy's semaglutide active pharmaceutical ingredient, which forced the company to suspend production of new batches of its generic version of Novo Nordisk's weight-loss drug Wegovy. The company sold just 180,000 semaglutide pens before halting supplies, according to Nirmal Bang analyst Niharika Agarwal.

Dr Reddy's booked a one-time provision of Rs 240 crore ($24.75 million) toward inventory and related costs from the disruption. Supplies in India and Canada — the only two markets where it has secured approval — will remain unavailable until at least late October, the company said earlier this month.

"We understood the chemistry and the root cause of the API impurity. We should be able to supply by November."

— Erez Israeli, CEO, Dr Reddy's Laboratories

The setback forced Dr Reddy's to slash its fiscal-year semaglutide sales target to 6-7 million pens from the 12 million estimated earlier. CEO Erez Israeli said Q2 would be entirely without semaglutide sales, with supplies resuming only in the third and fourth quarters. The disruption could also delay production scale-up by three to four months despite strong demand.

North America Revenue Collapse

Revenue from North America, Dr Reddy's largest market, plunged 35.3% to Rs 2,205 crore during the quarter. The decline was driven primarily by the end of the company's Lenalidomide agreement with the innovator, which had been a significant revenue contributor in the year-ago period. Pricing pressure and intensifying competition in the US generics market added to the headwinds.

Despite the revenue drop, Dr Reddy's continued building its US pipeline, launching six new products in the region and filing five Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs) and one New Drug Application (NDA) with the USFDA. As of June 30, the company had 79 filings pending approval, including 24 with potential "First to File" status.

Bright Spots Across Other Geographies

The underlying base business, excluding Lenalidomide, continued to deliver double-digit growth across all key geographies, the company said. Revenue from India rose 16.8% to Rs 1,720 crore, driven by new brand launches, recently acquired portfolios, price increases, and higher sales volumes.

Emerging markets delivered 31% revenue growth, led by new product launches and a 28% surge in Russia. Europe registered 13% growth, though generics pricing pressure and a change in operating model for the acquired NRT (nicotine replacement therapy) business moderated gains.

"Our Q1 FY27 performance reflected the expected transition beyond lenalidomide revenues, along with an unexpected impact related to semaglutide API. However, our underlying base business continued to deliver healthy double-digit growth across all key geographies."

— G V Prasad, Co-Chairman and Managing Director, Dr Reddy's

US Tariff Uncertainty Adds to Headwinds

Adding to the pressure on Dr Reddy's largest market, US President Donald Trump on Tuesday unveiled a phased tariff plan for imported generic medicines, giving drugmakers a two-year window before duties take effect. The announcement sent pharmaceutical stocks broadly lower, with the Nifty Pharma index trading in the red.

Israeli was blunt about the impracticality of relocating manufacturing. "It is not practical to move operations like that to the United States. And obviously, if tariffs are imposed, we'll have to raise prices," he said. He added that the company would consider investing in the US, but not in response to tariff pressure.

Looking Ahead

Dr Reddy's reported EBITDA margin of 12.5% for the quarter and a gross profit margin of 46.5%, down over 10 percentage points year-over-year. The company spent Rs 307 crore in capital expenditure during Q1 and has lined up Rs 1,800 crore in investment for the full fiscal year.

The company expects domestic semaglutide sales to grow broadly in line with the market's double-digit trajectory once supplies resume. It is also pursuing regulatory approvals in Brazil, Turkey, and Mexico, though the supply disruption could delay those market entries. Shares of Dr Reddy's settled 2.16% lower at Rs 1,179.90 on the NSE.

nri_angle: Dr Reddy's is listed on the NYSE (ticker RDY) and derives significant revenue from North America. New US tariffs on generic medicines and the company's semaglutide supply disruption directly affect drug availability and pricing for the Indian diaspora.
